'''unlimber<sup>2</sup>''' (un-lim′bėr), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''limber''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To detach the limbers from; take off the limbers of: as, to ''unlimber'' guns.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To detach the limbers from the guns.

'''unlimitable†''' (un-lim′i-ta-bl), ''a.'' Illimitable. ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxviii.

'''unlimited''' (un-lim′i-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not limited; having no bounds; boundless.
{{smaller block|So ''unlimited'' is our impotence . . . that it fetters our very wishes.
{{right|''Boyle.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''unlimited'', though perhaps not indefinite, modifiability of matter.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Invert., p. 41.}}}}
'''2.''' Undefined; indefinite; not bounded by proper exceptions.
{{smaller block|With gross and popular capacities, nothing doth more prevail than ''unlimited'' generalities, because of their plainness at the first sight.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.}}}}
'''3.''' Unconfined; not restrained; not restricted.
{{smaller block|An unguarded, ''unlimited'' will.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor.''}}}}

'''unless''' (un-les′), ''conj.'' [Early mod. E. also ''unlesse, onless, onlesse, onles'', earlier ''onlesse that, on lesse that'' (''that'' being ultimately dropped, as with ''for'', conj., ''lest'', etc.), a phrase analogous to ''at least, at most'', etc.: see ''on''<sup>1</sup> and ''less''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''lest''.] '''1.''' If it be not that; if it be not the case that; were it not the fact that; if . . . not; supposing that . . . not.
{{smaller block|It is not possible for all things to be well, ''unless'' all men were good: which I think will not be yet these good many years. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i.}}
<poem>''Unless'' thou tell’st me where thou had’st this ring,
Thou diest within this hour.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, v. 3. 284.}}
<poem>You should not ask, ’''less'' you knew how to give.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, ii. 1.}}}}
'''2†.''' For fear that; in case; lest.
{{smaller block|<poem>Beware you do not once the same gainsay,
''Unless'' with death he do your rashness pay.</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Alphonsus, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|[By omission of a verb, implied in the context, ''unless'' may have the force of ‘except,’ ‘but for’: as,
<poem>Here nothing breeds
''Unless'' the nightly owl.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 3. 97.}}
<poem>Let not wine,
''Unless'' in sacrifice or rites divine,</poem>}}
<poem>Be ever known of shepherds.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, v. 5.]}}}}

='''Syn.''' ''Except, Unless.'' ''Except'' could once be used as a synonym for ''unless'', but the words have now drawn entirely apart. ''Unless'' is only a conjunction; ''except'' is only a preposition. ''Except'' introduces an exception to a statement which is otherwise general: it may be followed by a clause when connection is made by a particle, as ''when, that, as, while'', or especially another preposition: the omission of such connective makes the structure archaic. ''Unless'' introduces a clause, or the abbreviation of a clause, indicating a limitation or condition.

{{smaller block|''Unletted'' of every wight. ''The Isle of Ladies'', l. 1831.}}

'''unlettered''' (un-let′ėrd), ''a.'' Unlearned; untaught; ignorant; illiterate. ''Milton'', Comus, l. 174.='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Illiterate, Unlearned'', etc. See ''ignorant.''}}

'''unletteredness''' (un-let′ėrd-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unlettered.

'''unleveful†''', ''a.'' [ME., also ''unleful, unlefful''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''leveful.''] Unlawful.
{{smaller block|I deme it felony and ''unleveful.''

<poem>A longyng ''vnleffull'' light in his hert
Gert hym hast in a hete, harmyt hym after.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 13686.}}}}

'''unlevel''' (un-lev′l), ''a.'' Not level; uneven.

'''unlevel''' (un-lev′l), ''v. t.'' To make not level or uneven. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It was so plain as there was scarcely any bush or hillock either to ''unlevel'' or shadow it.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.}}}}

'''unlicensed''' (un-lī′sẹnst), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not licensed; not having a license: as, an ''unlicensed'' innkeeper. —'''2.''' Done or undertaken without, or in defiance of, due license or permission: as, an ''unlicensed'' traffic.

'''unlicked''' (un-likt′), ''a.'' Not licked; not brought to proper shape by licking: from the old popular notion that the she-bear licked her cubs into shape; hence, ungainly; raw; unmannerly; uncultivated.
{{smaller block|A country squire, with the equipage of a wife and two daughters, . . . oh gad! two such ''unlicked'' cubs!
{{right|''Congreve'', Old Bachelor, iv. 8.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>First the sun,

'''unlike''' (un-līk′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unlic'', ''unlich'', ''unilich'', < AS. ''ungelīc'' (= OFries. ''unlīk'' = G. ''ungleich'' = Icel. ''ūlīkr'' = Sw. ''olik'' = Dan. ''ulig''), < ''un-'', not, + ''gelīc'', like: see ''like''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Not like; dissimilar; diverse; having no resemblance.
{{smaller block|<poem>What occasion of import
Hath all so long detain’d you from your wife,
And sent you hither so ''unlike'' yourself?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 2. 106.}}}}

{{smaller block|It ne is nat an ''unlyk'' myracle to hem that ne knowen it nat.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iv. prose 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is not ''vnlike'' that the Britons accompanied the Cimbrians and Gaules in those expeditions.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Unlike quantities''', in ''math.'', quantities expressed by different letters or combinations of letters, or by the same letters with different exponents.—'''Unlike signs''', the signs ''plus'' (+) and ''minus'' (—).}}

'''unlike''' (un-līk′), ''adv.'' Not in a like or similar manner; not like or as.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oft have I seen the haughty cardinal . . .
Swear like a ruffian and demean himself
''Unlike'' the ruler of a commonweal.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., i. 1. 189.}}}}

'''unlikelihood''' (un-līk′li-hu̇d), ''n.'' The state of being unlikely or improbable; improbability.
{{smaller block|Thus much may suffice to shew the ''vnlikelihood'' or rather impossibilitie of the supposed comming of our Saxon ancestors from elsewhere into Germanie.
{{right|''Verstegan'', Rest. of Decayed Intelligence (ed. 1628), p. 39.}}}}
{{smaller block|The extreme ''unlikelihood'' that such men should engage in such a measure.
{{right|''Paley'', Evidences, iii. 8.}}}}

'''unlikeliness''' (un-līk′li-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unlyklynesse''; < ''unlikely'' + ''-ness''.] '''1.''' The state of being unlikely; improbability.
{{smaller block|There are degrees herein, from the very neighbourhood of demonstration quite down to improbability and ''unlikeliness''.
{{right|''Locke''.}}}}
'''2.''' The state of being unlike; dissimilarity. ''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, Christ’s Baptism.
{{smaller block|Strange in its utter ''unlikeliness'' to any teaching, Platonist or Hebrew.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Hypatia, xxi.}}}}
'''3†.''' Unattractiveness; the incapacity to excite liking or love.
<poem>I that God of Loves servaunts serve,
Ne dar to love for myn ''unliklynesse.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 16.}}}}

'''unlikely''' (un-līk′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unlikely'', ''unlikly''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''likely''.] '''1.''' Such as cannot be reasonably expected; improbable: as, an ''unlikely'' event.
{{smaller block|That it wrung his conscience to condemn the Earle of high Treason is not ''unlikely''. ''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, ii.}}
'''2.''' Not holding out a prospect of success or of a desired result; likely to fail; unpromising.
{{smaller block|A very ''unlikely'' envy she hath stumbled upon against the princess’s unspeakable beauty.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, ii.}}
<poem>A strange ''unlikely'' errand, sure, is thine.</poem>
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Balder Dead, I. 83.}}}}
'''3†.''' Not calculated to inspire liking or affection; not likable or lovable.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whan I considere youre beautee,
And therwithal the ''unlikly'' elde of me.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 936.}}}}

'''unlikely''' (un-līk′li), ''adv.'' In an unlikely manner; with no or little likelihood; improbably.
{{smaller block|The pleasures . . . not ''unlikely'' may proceed from the discoveries each shall communicate to another. ''Pope.''}}

'''unliken†''' (un-lī′kn), ''v. t.'' To make unlike; feign; pretend. ''Wyclif.''

'''unlikeness''' (un-līk′nes), ''n.'' Want of resemblance; dissimilarity.
{{smaller block|<poem>And he supplied my want the more
As his ''unlikeness'' fitted mine.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, lxxix.}}}}
